newsitem.title: GERMANY: FDP warns partners not to strain Bonn coalition.
newsitem.headline: FDP warns partners not to strain Bonn coalition.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt warned the partners of his liberal Free Democrat Party on Sunday that the Bonn coalition would be at risk if they again called into question a tax cut agreed for 1998.

Rexrodt's comments added fuel to a spat between the Free Democrats (FDP) and Finance Minister Theo Waigel's conservative CSU, which has threatened to flare up again over the FDP's persistant demands for cuts in the so-called solidarity tax.
Both parties are junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government.
"The cut in the solidarity tax is a part of the FDP's identity, it's an essential in the coalition," Rexrodt told Monday's daily Bild, according to an advance release on Sunday.
"We cannot afford another delay in the reduction of the solidarity tax, and we will not (accept one)."

But Waigel rounded on the FDP for harping on the widely resented tax, a 7.5 percent levy on income tax intended to finance German unification by the year 2000, and told it to come up with ways of making up for the fall in revenues.

The FDP has staked its political credibility on tax cuts. It had already fought bitterly to keep a two point cut in the tax from January 1998, after Waigel decided a strapped budget meant the cut could not go ahead as planned in mid-1997.
Since securing that pledge, the FDP has angered its coalition partners by going on to demand its complete abolition.
"There is no point trying to stimulate the economy with a major tax reform while retaining the solidarity tax," Rexrodt said. "The solidarity tax must go by the year 2000."
But Waigel, chairman of the Bavarian-based Christian Social Union (CSU), said he had not heard a word from the FDP about how this drop in government revenue was to be made up.
"It's not possible to get rid of the solidarity surcharge in one go at the same time as reforming the tax system," he told NTV television news.

"It's no solution to say we'll scrap the tax from a certain date without any substitute, without saying how to make up the gap of almost 30 billion marks ($19 billion) in the budget," he said. ($1=1.5492 Mark)
